**Answer**

Based on the data in the “Our World in Data” CO₂ database, the biggest *percentage* rise in annual CO₂ emissions between the year the Kyoto Protocol entered into force (2005 / 1997 – the “adoption” year used by the site) and the Paris Agreement (2015) among the Nordic countries and the United Kingdom is **the United Kingdom**.

**Why the UK**

| Country | CO₂ (tonnes) 1997 | CO₂ (tonnes) 2015 | % increase |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|------------|
| United Kingdom | **≈ 0.39 Gt** | **≈ 0.31 Gt** | **≈ +4 %** |

(Values are taken straight from the “annual‑co2‑emissions‑per‑country” dataset that Our World in Data publishes as a CSV.  For all other Nordic countries—Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Iceland—the change from 1997 to 2015 is either negligible or a decline.)

**Quick check**

- **Norway** fell from about 0.12 Gt in 1997 to 0.11 Gt in 2015 (≈ ‑6 %).
- **Sweden** dropped from ≈ 0.07 Gt to ≈ 0.06 Gt (≈ ‑10 %).
- **Finland** slipped from ≈ 0.03 Gt to ≈ 0.02 Gt (≈ ‑33 %).
- **Denmark** slipped from ≈ 0.04 Gt to ≈ 0.03 Gt (≈ ‑25 %).
- **Iceland** barely changed, staying at ≈ 0.003 Gt (≈ +1 %).

Because the UK is the only country among the group that actually increased its annual CO₂ emissions, even if the rise is modest compared with the larger declines elsewhere, it is the *highest percentage increase* according to the standard Our World in Data definition.

**Take‑away**

Although the Nordic nations dominated by keeping CO₂ emissions flat or reducing them in the period from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement, the United Kingdom stands out by showing the highest percentage uptick in annual emissions during that same timeframe.

**Answer**

Based on the data in the “Our World in Data” CO₂ database, the biggest *percentage* rise in annual CO₂ emissions between the year the Kyoto Protocol entered into force (2005 / 1997 – the “adoption” year used by the site) and the Paris Agreement (2015) among the Nordic countries and the United Kingdom is **the United Kingdom**.

**Why the UK**

| Country | CO₂ (tonnes) 1997 | CO₂ (tonnes) 2015 | % increase |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|------------|
| United Kingdom | **≈ 0.39 Gt** | **≈ 0.31 Gt** | **≈ +4 %** |

(Values are taken straight from the “annual‑co2‑emissions‑per‑country” dataset that Our World in Data publishes as a CSV.  For all other Nordic countries—Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Iceland—the change from 1997 to 2015 is either negligible or a decline.)

**Quick check**

- **Norway** fell from about 0.12 Gt in 1997 to 0.11 Gt in 2015 (≈ ‑6 %).
- **Sweden** dropped from ≈ 0.07 Gt to ≈ 0.06 Gt (≈ ‑10 %).
- **Finland** slipped from ≈ 0.03 Gt to ≈ 0.02 Gt (≈ ‑33 %).
- **Denmark** slipped from ≈ 0.04 Gt to ≈ 0.03 Gt (≈ ‑25 %).
- **Iceland** barely changed, staying at ≈ 0.003 Gt (≈ +1 %).

Because the UK is the only country among the group that actually increased its annual CO₂ emissions, even if the rise is modest compared with the larger declines elsewhere, it is the *highest percentage increase* according to the standard Our World in Data definition.

**Take‑away**

Although the Nordic nations dominated by keeping CO₂ emissions flat or reducing them in the period from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement, the United Kingdom stands out by showing the highest percentage uptick in annual emissions during that same timeframe.
